I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed redistricting plan, specifically the decision to divide the Ford’s Colony neighborhood. Splitting established communities—particularly at the elementary level— unnecessarily disrupts the academic and social stability of students. Children rely on consistent peer groups and support networks, and this proposal would dismantle those relationships without sufficient justification. In addition, the district should implement a clearly defined “grace period” allowing 5th, 8th, and 12th graders to remain at their current schools to complete their final year. Forcing students to transition to a new school during a critical milestone year is both disruptive and avoidable. These are pivotal stages in a student’s academic and social development, and stability during this time should be a priority. There is clear precedent for this approach. When Grafton High School opened in York County in 1996, it did not include a senior class; the first graduating class was in 1998. Students already in their final years were allowed to remain at their existing schools to complete their education. This reflects a recognition that continuity for students in milestone years outweighs the administrative convenience of immediate boundary changes. The same student- centered approach should be applied here. Furthermore, the argument that a grace period cannot be accommodated due to transportation constraints is not consistent with current practice. The district’s own data shows that students already attend schools outside of their zoned areas under various circumstances. Dr. Keever acknowledged that transportation exceptions exist, yet indicated reluctance to extend a similar consideration for a limited, one-year grace period. This inconsistency is difficult to justify, particularly when the requested accommodation is both temporary and narrowly focused. School transitions are inherently challenging. Requiring students in their final year of elementary or middle school to leave their established environment adds unnecessary academic and emotional strain. This is a preventable outcome. The district has both the precedent and the flexibility to act in the best interest of its students. I urge you to reconsider both the division of established neighborhoods and the lack of a transition plan for students in their final year. These decisions have real and lasting impacts on children and should reflect a commitment to stability, fairness, and student well-being.

t.additional: I am writing to express serious concerns regarding the proposed redistricting plan and the impact it will have on families in Ford’s Colony. While I understand that boundary adjustments are sometimes necessary, I believe several aspects of this proposal unnecessarily disrupt students and families without providing reasonable transition accommodations. First, the proposal would split established neighborhoods within Ford’s Colony into different elementary school zones. Numerous studies have shown that maintaining neighborhood and peer continuity is important for children’s academic, social, and emotional development. Students benefit when they attend school with the peers they grow up with, participate in community activities with, and rely on for social support. Research consistently shows that school transitions and disruptions to peer networks can negatively affect student belonging, academic performance, and emotional well-being — particularly for elementary-aged children. Neighborhood schools are not simply buildings; they are community anchors. Splitting long-established neighborhoods weakens community cohesion, creates unnecessary social fragmentation among children, and places additional stress on families trying to maintain friendships, carpools, extracurricular participation, and community involvement. Second, I am deeply disappointed that the district is unwilling to provide even a recommendation to the school board for a limited one-year open-enrollment or grandfathering option for students in key transition grades unless transportation is provided by the district. I am not asking for permanent open enrollment. I am simply asking for reasonable flexibility for students who are nearing the completion of a major educational milestone: 5th graders finishing elementary school, 8th graders finishing middle school, and 12th graders finishing high school. Forcing students to leave their school community during these pivotal years is unnecessarily disruptive. Many school districts across the country provide transition exceptions or grandfathering opportunities during rezoning processes, often with the understanding that families provide their own transportation. This approach balances district logistical concerns with the educational and emotional stability of students. I find it inequitable that families willing to assume transportation responsibility are not even being offered this option. A one-year grace period would impose minimal long-term impact on the district while significantly easing the transition burden on affected students and families. Currently, we have students living in one school zone attending another for special reasons. These students are not offered transportation and the expectation should be the same for this one-year open enrollment transition period. At a time when student mental health, school connectedness, and community engagement are being emphasized nationwide, this proposal appears to move in the opposite direction. I strongly urge the Board to reconsider: The decision to split Ford’s Colony into separate elementary school zones; and The refusal to offer a limited grandfathering/open-enrollment option for students in transition grades whose families can provide transportation. I respectfully ask the Board to place greater value on stability, continuity, and the social well-being of students as these decisions are finalized. Thank you for your consideration.

I would also like to express concern regarding the process for gathering community feedback on the proposed redistricting plan. While I appreciate that the district has scheduled community forums, it appears the only method for submitting detailed written feedback is through a single open-ended question at the end of a private survey. For a decision that will significantly impact students, families, and neighborhoods, this feels limiting and lacks transparency. Additionally, the district has stated that the current maps are only draft proposals and are intended to evolve based on community feedback. However, it is my understanding that there are currently no plans to hold additional community forums if or when revised maps are released. That seems inconsistent with the collaborative and iterative process the district has described. If substantial revisions are made to attendance boundaries, families should have an opportunity to review, discuss, and respond to those updated proposals in a public setting before final decisions are made. Otherwise, community input is effectively limited to reacting to only the initial drafts, rather than participating in a truly iterative feedback process. I believe families would benefit from a more open and visible way to review community feedback and concerns throughout this process. Allowing residents to see the themes, concerns, and perspectives being raised by others would help foster a more informed and collaborative discussion surrounding these important decisions. A more transparent and iterative feedback process would help build trust and reassure families that community concerns are being fully heard and considered before final decisions are made. Thank you for your consideration.

t.opinion: Up until this point, the division has done a good job of keeping neighborhoods together and fostering a community feeling within the school system.
t.critical: The most critical issue with the proposed plan is the decision to split children from the same Fords Colony neighborhoods into two separate elementary schools. This unnecessarily divides young children during the earliest and most formative years of their education and disrupts the strong community networks that families rely on every day. In neighborhoods like ours, families depend heavily on one another for carpools, childcare support, after-school activities, emergency coverage, and social connection. These relationships are built around children attending the same schools together. Separating elementary-aged children across different schools weakens those support systems and fractures long-established community ties. The proposal also appears to insufficiently account for the broader socioeconomic impacts these changes could create. Boundary decisions affect far more than enrollment numbers and building capacity. They influence property values, neighborhood stability, school culture, family engagement, and the overall attractiveness of communities to current and future residents. These impacts deserve far more consideration and transparency than they have received throughout this process. Equally concerning has been the lack of meaningful collaboration and open dialogue with the community. Many families feel the process has been largely top-down, with limited opportunities for genuine discussion, alternative scenario exploration, or clear explanation regarding how feedback will influence outcomes. Community engagement should involve active partnership and transparency, not simply collecting comments after major proposals have already been developed. Families want to feel heard and included in decisions that will significantly affect their children and communities for years to come.

The consulting firm presents one proposed map for elementary, middle, and high school that shows they lazily drew lines around each school (except in the middle of the district, where they made carve outs), didn't follow most of the guiding principles, and no one on the school board said, "Please go back to the drawing board”? Was the school board trying to gauge community interest for segregation in 2026, or is this an expensive joke? Around 54% of the elementary school students in our district come from lower-income families; however, seven out of nine of our elementary schools are Title 1 schools (78%)…..SEVEN OUT OF NINE! The proposed maps put more students from lower-income families into the Title 1 schools during a time where federal funding for Title 1 schools is decreasing in Virginia! There’s clearly room for some of elementary schools to decrease their number of students from lower-income families (i.e., CBB, JBB), especially when the two non-Title 1 schools have less than 27% of students from lower-income families! On top of moving more children from lower- income families into Title 1 schools, the maps propose moving students from Ford's Colony that are currently attending DJ to Matoaka? I'm sorry, but a school that already raises almost $30,000 in OCTOBER for their annual Walk-A-Thon (Matoaka), does not need more students from middle class, upper middle class, or rich families while the rest of the schools struggle to do ANYTHING. Please go back to the drawing board!

Why did our district approve a $150,000 contract to MGT to review boundary lines, when Madison, WI only paid $90,000 in 2025? There are over 25,000 students in the Madison, WI district and over 50 public schools, yet we paid significantly more! https://captimes.com/news/education/madison-schools-face-segregated-reality- redrawing-attendance-maps/article_e68e6bd1-3306-4670-b4fe-c5a3b1e0bc4c.html

t.critical: The proposed redistricting plan raises serious concerns about equity, socioeconomic balance, and the district’s responsibility to provide fair educational opportunities for all students. By concentrating lower-income neighborhoods into one school while higher-income neighborhoods are grouped into another, the district is effectively creating a system of economic segregation. Whether intentional or not, the outcome is the same: one school will bear a disproportionate share of economic hardship, while the other benefits from greater financial stability, parental resources, fundraising capacity, and social capital. Research consistently shows that economically diverse schools produce stronger academic and social outcomes for all students. Diverse learning environments foster broader perspectives, greater opportunity, and more equitable access to experienced teachers, advanced coursework, extracurricular programs, and community support. Separating students along socioeconomic lines undermines these goals and sends a damaging message about whose needs and opportunities matter most. This proposal does not reflect a commitment to equity. Equity is not simply about drawing lines on a map; it is about ensuring that all students have meaningful access to the same quality of education, support systems, and opportunities for success. A redistricting plan that intensifies economic disparities between schools works directly against that principle. I strongly urge the district to reconsider this proposal and prioritize boundary solutions that maintain socioeconomic balance rather than deepen divisions between communities. Public schools should bring communities together, not reinforce inequality through district policy.

t.positive: A potential benefit of the elementary school scenario is better balancing of enrollment across schools. However, in our case, it would negatively impact my children by moving our neighborhood farther from our current school and disrupting established rou
t.concern: The biggest concern is that the scenario shifts entire neighborhoods, including mine (Jamestown 1607 townhomes), out of our current school zone. This increases travel distance, disrupts established peer groups, and creates unnecessary instability for stud
t.additional: I appreciate the Division’s effort to address enrollment balance, facility use, and long-term growth. However, I am concerned that the current scenarios do not fully account for the impact on specific neighborhoods like mine. The Jamestown 1607 townhomes have consistently been part of the Laurel Lane pathway for years, even though we are near the boundary, and this longstanding alignment has worked well for our community. The proposed changes would move our entire neighborhood out of that pathway and assign students to a middle school that is significantly farther away. Currently, the middle school in our existing pathway is approximately 12 minutes away, while the proposed reassignment would increase travel time to over 20 minutes. This creates clear logistical challenges, including longer daily commutes, increased reliance on transportation, and less time for students to participate in extracurricular activities, complete homework, and maintain balanced routines. In addition to the transportation impact, this change also disrupts established peer groups and continuity for students who have progressed together through the same school pathway. Maintaining our current alignment with Laurel Lane supports both proximity and stability, which are key to student success and well-being. I would ask that the Division more closely consider proximity, travel time, and continuity when finalizing boundaries, especially for neighborhoods that are already well-aligned with their schools. Maintaining shorter travel times and keeping student groups together should remain a priority. One question I still have is how the Division is weighing transportation distance and travel time versus capacity balancing, and whether adjustments can be made to minimize the impact on communities like ours. My recommendation would be to revise the scenarios to keep neighborhoods intact where possible and avoid reassigning students to significantly farther schools when there are reasonable alternatives.

t.critical: While there are several concerns within this proposal, tonight I want to focus on the decision to divide our neighborhood at the elementary school level. These are young children who currently walk, bike, and ride buses to school together while growing up side by side in a close-knit community. As working parents, we depend heavily on those relationships and daily support systems for carpools, childcare, after-school pickups, transportation to activities, and the overall balance of work and family life.

t.additional: Although I have deep concerns over all three levels of education I am going to focus on just the high school currently specifically Lafayette of which my After reviewing the presentation from MGT, the data indicates that Lafayette High School is projected to experience the most negative impact under the proposed boundary scenario based on enrollment growth, facility age, and future funding allocation. - [ ] Under the current boundary configuration, Lafayette is projected to experience only a 3.2% increase in capacity utilization by SY2035. However, under the proposed configuration, utilization is projected to increase by 8.6%, pushing the school beyond 100% capacity by SY2035- Despite this projected growth, Lafayette is slated to receive the smallest future capital investment and currently has no major expansion projects planned to accommodate the increase in enrollment. - [ ] Lafayette High School already has the lowest graduation and college readiness rates in WJCC, and increasing enrollment without corresponding expansion or investment raises serious concerns about academics, class sizes, student well-being, safety, and the overall impact of overcrowding. - [ ] Conversely-Jamestown High School is projected to remain the smallest-capacity high school in the division and operate at only 77% capacity by SY2035 under the proposed configuration all while having a capital improvement plan of $11M in future investments, including cafeteria expansion, construction, and design improvements. Why is the division prioritizing significant expansion funding at a school projected to remain substantially under capacity, while a much older school with comparable physical size is expected to exceed capacity within the next decade with comparatively limited investment? This stark disparity is highly concerning if the stated purpose of MGT’s analysis was to address and improve boundary balance and capacity issues across all of WJC and that is only toughing on one small comparison between two out of 16 schools within WJCC. I struggle to see any positive outcome from these proposed changes. In my view, they create significant demographic imbalances and risk creating the perception of economic and racial separation within our school system. Currently, Jamestown High School would become the least diverse high school, with only 27% diversity and 22% economically disadvantaged students, while Lafayette High School and Warhill High School remain much closer to a balanced 50/50 demographic distribution. That raises an important question: how can a school division that emphasizes diversity, equity, and inclusion support a plan that creates one of the least diverse schools in the district — while also directing the largest taxpayer-funded investment, $11 million, into that same school?

But I also don't like that LHS doesn't have soap in the bathrooms, or that my son's team is trying to raise money for a Porta Potty at the track because the school doesn't have one for practices. I want to make sure LHS can have the resources they need to help kids in less-than-desirable home lives know that they are valued. I don't want those kids to experience broken windows syndrome or think because they aren't white that their school has to feel like a prison without access to the outdoors or windows. However, I want to make sure the other kids at LHS can know they are worth it and they aren't just getting kept together with other kids that struggle to be forgotten. How will we make sure these kids know that they are valued and important and worth it? Why are these kids being put in the building that is the most prison-like? How can we get LHS to be a building we can be proud to showcase? We do love LHS. Again, we don't want to be at a different school (okay, honestly, the building stinks, but the school entity is wonderful - we have loved the staff and administration there). Would LHS receive more resource allocation to pay for better teachers and coaches with it being lower income? I certainly hope so. Thank you so much - I know you all are trying to do your best for everyone. I hope you can make sure those families that may not have the resources to speak up for themselves can be heard, and it's not just squeaky voices from Kingsmill and Fords Colony that get heard. Please make sure those students with no money also get a fair chance - these kids are amazing!

t.additional: Consider the human impact---the people at the heart of these changes. The classes of 2029-2032 are most impacted by the middle and high school changes and were the most affected by the 2020-2021 hybrid model, when they were aged 5-9. They missed out on many social skill development opportunities at school and in the community, in addition to quality in-person instruction. Have you looked at your academic and attendance data specifically for these cohorts? Allow families to finish middle and high school where they start instead of moving students after they finally adjust to their middle or high school. Consider a phased in model to address the PreK centers and Elementary zones first. Families who may want to move to maintain their zones, aka school communities, are stuck in an stagnant economy and housing market. Families who were already struggling with limited social, familial, and financial resources cannot move, and the tweens and teens who would have to move would need extra support in their schools. The middle and high schools are already struggling with vapes(!!!), fights, attendance, apathy, teacher training and support, etc. Do you have a plan to put in place supports for the most at-risk families? These families are hiding in plain sight and ignored by the community's overwhelming focus on middle and upper middle class families. The double and triple shift of some communities is really unfortunate. The shift of students mid-way through middle or high school does not consider the needs of this age group. The presentation and data are solid but you forget that schools are in the people business.

t.additional: My name is and I am a -grade student at Warhill High School. I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed redistricting plan. While I understand that changes like this may be necessary, I strongly believe that juniors and seniors, particularly those in the Class of 2028 and 2029, should not be required to change schools. Many of these students have attended their current school since their freshman year. Over that time, they have built strong friendships, connections with teachers, and a sense of belonging within their school community. Requiring them to leave and adjust to a new environment during their final years of high school does not seem fair. This issue is especially important for student-athletes and those involved in extracurricular activities. Many students have worked extremely hard to build their skills, earn positions on teams, and establish a reputation within their school. If they are required to transfer, they may have to start over from the beginning, losing opportunities they have worked toward for years. Being so close to achieving personal and team goals, only to have those opportunities disrupted, could be very discouraging. I respectfully ask that juniors and seniors be given the option to remain at their current school if they choose, even if that requires them to arrange their own transportation. Offering this choice would help protect the time, effort, and dedication students have already invested. Additionally, I believe the redistricting process could be implemented more gradually to reduce disruption. For example, the changes could initially apply only to incoming freshmen and possibly sophomores, as well as middle and elementary school students. Over time, this would allow for a smoother transition and minimize the impact on students who are closer to graduating. High school is an important stage before entering the real world, and stability during these years is essential. I also believe that simply redistributing students among existing schools may not fully solve the issue. Based on what has been shared, some schools are already near or at capacity. Moving students around may temporarily balance numbers, but it could lead to overcrowding in other schools. A more long-term solution may be to consider building a new high school. While I understand this would be expensive, student populations are continuing to grow, and this issue may arise again in the future. Investing in additional school facilities could better support students and the community over time. Thank you for taking the time to consider my perspective. I hope you will take into account how these changes may affect students and allow for options that support their success. If you have any questions or would like to discuss my ideas further, please feel free to contact me at Sincerely, June 1, 2026

t.additional: I am concerned that the proposed redistricting raises serious equity concerns without clearly advancing the district’s stated goals. The proposal appears to increase the concentration of socioeconomic disadvantage at some schools while significantly changing the socioeconomic and racial composition of others. In particular, moving Kingsmill and Kingspoint to Laurel Lane would likely substantially alter Laurel Lane’s current student body, reduce its existing diversity, and potentially affect the school’s Title I status. If Laurel Lane were to lose Title I eligibility, that could have serious consequences for students who currently depend on schoolwide supports, including free breakfast and lunch. At the same time, the proposal appears to concentrate greater socioeconomic need at Mathews Whaley while removing some of the neighborhoods that have historically helped support that school community. This could weaken PTA involvement, volunteer networks, family engagement, enrichment opportunities, and overall school stability. I do not feel the district has fully answered several important questions: Why are these changes considered acceptable tradeoffs? Has the district analyzed the impact on Laurel Lane’s Title I status? How many students could lose access to schoolwide supports? What specific supports would be provided to schools with increased need? How would the district measure whether those supports are enough? And what happens if the plan makes existing inequities worse? Before moving forward, I believe the district needs to clearly explain the long-term impact on affected schools and communities and show how it will prevent this proposal from deepening inequities across the division.

t.additional: I believe there is a strong opportunity for the district to consider building a new high school in the northern part of the county to better support our growing student population. In conjunction with that, repurposing Lafayette as a dedicated CTE center could be a strategic and impactful use of existing resources. Board, MGT: I am a member of this community, and I am not against redistricting. I’m writing in support of doing redistricting well. The two new Bright Beginnings pre-K centers are a genuine good, and consolidating pre-K will free real classroom space. The growth in the north of the county is real. Some of the current feeder patterns and island zones plainly need fixing. Those are legitimate reasons to redraw boundaries, and the division is right to take them seriously. My objection is narrower and, I hope, harder to dismiss: by the division's own data, these specific draft maps make our most segregated and highest-need schools more segregated and higher-need — and they do so while failing a guiding principle this Board itself adopted. These effects, in this moment – the resegregation of our schools and further disadvantaging our children and families – and their measures are not ones our community will stand for. I am asking the Board to: 1 Pause the timeline immediately. By the division's own schedule there is no emergency. 2 Reject these first draft maps as the basis for any future recommendations and especially a final recommendation. 3 Adopt "Demographics" as an explicitly weighted principle and publish a written equity impact analysis — school by school, on poverty, diversity, English-learner, and special-education concentration — before any further process, progress, maps, refinement, or vote. 4 Hold a genuine, public, two-way Q&A before a recommendation goes to the Board. Every number that follows is the division's own. 1. By the division's own data, these maps concentrate need. MGT's "Utilization and Demographics — Residence-Based Statistical Report" gives the before-and-after demographics for every school on four measures — economically disadvantaged (EcDis), diversity, English- language learners (ELL), and students with IEPs — and even pre-computes the difference. The pattern in that table is textbook concentration: the schools that already serve the most need are assigned more, and the schools that serve the least are assigned less. At the elementary level, economic disadvantage rises at the schools already carrying the most: • James River — already the division's highest-poverty elementary at 57.0% — rises to 63.9% (+6.9), with diversity rising to 60.1% and English-learners to 40.2%. • D.J. Montague rises from 39.2% to 51.3% EcDis (+12.1), with diversity +11.5 and IEP +6.5. • Matthew Whaley rises from 45.7% to 54.3% (+8.6). • Clara Byrd Baker rises +6.1. And it falls at the schools already carrying the least: • Matoaka drops from 24.8% to 16.8% (−8.0). • Laurel Lane drops from 33.5% to 28.2% (−5.3). • Stonehouse drops to 19.8% (−4.2); Norge sheds diversity (−3.7). Four measures, every one of them moving the wrong way at the wrong schools. These are MGT's figures, not mine. I am grateful to the Village Initiative for surfacing them; I have checked their numbers against MGT's table, and every one matches the consultant's own report exactly. 2. You can see the mechanism on the division's own map: Kingsmill. This is not an abstraction. On the division's own interactive draft-scenario map, Kingsmill — one of the most affluent neighborhoods in the area — is reassigned out of James River, the division's highest-poverty elementary, and into lower-poverty Laurel Lane. The legend confirms it (James River shaded cyan in the current boundaries; Kingsmill Neck shaded as a Laurel Lane "Potential Impact Area," study areas O and U, in the draft). By MGT's own figures this is exactly the kind of move that drives the swing the report shows: James River's economic-disadvantage share rising 6.9 points to 63.9% while Laurel Lane's falls 5.3 points to 28.2%. Moving wealth out of the poorest school and into a richer one necessarily concentrates poverty in the poorest school. The map and the table agree. 3. This fails the Board's own "Demographics" principle. In June 2025 the Board discussed, and in December 2025 affirmed, six guiding principles for this process. The second is Demographics: "Consider racial and ethnic diversity, as well as socioeconomic indicators, within schools" (Community Forum presentation, guiding-principles slide). That is the Board's own language, and it is co- equal with utilization. Yet by the division's own data, every demographic measure moves the wrong way at the highest-need schools. So one of two things happened: either the Demographics principle was not actually applied to the maps, or it was applied and then quietly overridden by the others. Frankly, I’m not sure which is worse. The superintendent's own framing — that no one principle outranks another and that they "push and pull" against each other — is, in effect, a concession that demographics can be outweighed, and here it was. That is a discretionary choice. I am asking – no, challenging – the Board to make that choice transparently, in writing, instead of letting it disappear into a static data table. This matters because of how the process was presented from the very beginning, and in the recent presentations. The roughly 90-minute forum – if you want to call it that – and the map design itself were built around capacity, "clean" lines, island zones, feeder patterns, and transportation. Demographics appeared as a residence-based table to be disclosed, not as an objective the maps were engineered to satisfy. MGT's lead presenter, Dr. Lance Richards, told the room that demographics and "economic factors, all of those are in the background around this conversation" (recorded forum, ~35:00). Disclosed in a table is not the same as weighed in the design. The Board named Demographics a principle; the maps were not built to honor it. 4. These maps reverse a recent, deliberate equity decision at James Blair. When WJCC last redistricted at scale, in 2018, to open James Blair Middle School, socioeconomic balance was an explicit guiding factor, and the division brought every school to roughly 87% utilization or below. The current draft moves James Blair the other way: economic disadvantage +10.5 (to 42.3%), diversity +9.2 (to 50.7%), and students with IEPs +8.5 (to 30.7%) — while Hornsby Middle sheds need on every measure (EcDis −8.3, diversity −5.8, IEP −4.7). The division has signaled it is changing the criteria it used in 2018. The Board should decide, openly, whether undoing that balance is really what it intends. 5. The process was flawed from the start — intentionally or not — and the capacity rationale does not hold up by the division's own numbers. The maps are justified by capacity. But the division's own forecast shows the capacity problem is narrow, the proposed fix is non-durable, and the long-term capacity solution the division once called "urgent" has quietly disappeared from the capital plan. It's narrow. By the division's own forum data, only three of nine elementary schools are over capacity — Stonehouse, Matthew Whaley, and D.J. Montague — and 64% of all projected new housing growth is in the Stonehouse attendance area alone. A capacity problem concentrated in three schools in the north is being addressed with a demographic reshuffle across the entire division, further punishing historically disadvantaged children and families. It's non-durable. Even under the plan, by MGT's own utilization forecast, Stonehouse returns to 100% of capacity by 2035 — full again within the forecast window. And the plan pushes Jamestown High over capacity on day one: from 94% today to 103% in 2027, worse than the status quo, before settling later. Lafayette High is driven to 101% by 2035 under the plan. A division-wide reshuffle justified by utilization leaves multiple buildings at or over capacity inside the same forecast. The real fix was dropped. A previous adopted capital plan stated that elementary enrollment was "at 98% of the capacity and is projected to be at more than 100% by FY2026, thus indicating an urgent need for a tenth (10th) Elementary school" (FY2020-29 CIP), estimated at about $38.5 million; the division's own newsroom called the new elementary school one of "the most critical capital issues" in that plan. That tenth elementary school is gone from the current adopted FY25-34 capital plan. What the current plan does fund is a Jamestown High School Expansion (design $785,000 in FY30; construction $7.856 million in FY31) and a Warhill High School Capacity Expansion ($11.61 million in FY31) — high-school capacity — plus the pre-K centers, a new central office, and storage. There is not one dollar of new elementary capacity, and not one dollar of capacity at Stonehouse, where the division's own forecast puts 64% of the growth; Stonehouse's only capital items are maintenance. So the localized, real, north-county elementary problem is being solved not by building elementary capacity where the children actually are, but by redrawing demographic boundaries division-wide — a fix that, by the division's own forecast, expires by 2035 and lands hardest on the students already carrying the most. Whether or not that was anyone's intent, that is a process that went wrong at the premise. America has long been intentionally biased towards those doing the measuring, who have the most education, who own the land, who hold the wealth, and hold the power, and this community, in this, our 250th year, will not go backwards. 6. This community already set a higher standard. Two years ago, when this community studied splitting into separate divisions, the feasibility studies treated demographics as a first-order concern — explicitly tying student demographics to achievement and to Title I, II, and III federal funding, and naming economic disparity, diversity, and English-learner support as key considerations. (The studies also documented the underlying divide: roughly 33% economic disadvantage in James City County versus about 52% in the City of Williamsburg.) Some of you are new here, but this community learned a lot about itself these past few years, and we chose to hold ourselves to a higher bar in 2024. We will not go backwards, we will not effectively redline our children, whatever you’d prefer the lines on the map to look like. This process should not assume we have forgotten what we learned, or be held to a lower bar. 7. There is no emergency. A pause costs nothing. By the division's own timeline – one that, outside of the pre-K adjustments, seems arbitrary in comparison to the effect: the survey closes June 7, 2026; a recommendation does not reach the Board until October 2026; implementation is not until the 2027-28 school year. MGT itself has said its three-year forecasts are reliable while longer ones are "assumptions on assumptions." There is ample time to add the equity analysis the Board's own principle requires. And the engagement so far has been one-directional: the forum was about 90 minutes of presentation followed by a live poll and a survey, and the superintendent stated plainly, "We're not going to do a Q&A," offering only individual conversations afterward. A decision that reshapes which children sit beside which children deserves a public, on-the-record, two-way conversation. A decision that — by design, whatever the reason — further harms the same children most affected by COVID school closures cannot and will not go without challenge. 8. The ask, concretely. 1 Pause the current timeline — there is no operational deadline before August 2027. 2 Reject these first draft maps and the process on which they were built as the basis for this and any future recommendation. 3 Re-run the process with Demographics as an explicitly weighted principle, and publish a written equity impact analysis before any vote — school by school, covering poverty/Title I concentration, English-learner and IEP concentration, the differentiated-instruction workload this creates for teachers, and resource disparities such as PTA fundraising. 4 Evaluate a capacity-addition alternative that puts elementary capacity where the growth actually is (the north/Stonehouse area), rather than absorbing localized overcrowding through a division-wide demographic reshuffle — including revisiting the tenth elementary school the division once called "urgent." 5 Commit, in writing, not to raise any school's economic-disadvantage or segregation level without a stated public justification you agree and are willing to defend live, in public. 6 Hold a genuine, public Q&A before any future recommendations are drafted or released, much less recommended to the Board. I am not asking the Board to stop planning for growth. I am asking it to honor this community’s history, our growth, the board’s own principle, to use its own data, and not solve a problem in the north of the county by deepening segregation across the entire division. Thank you.

t.critical: Proposed maps maps make our most segregated and highest-need schools more segregated and higher-need — and they do so while failing a guiding principle the Board itself adopted.
t.concern: 1. By the division's own data, these maps concentrate need. MGT's "Utilization and Demographics — Residence-Based Statistical Report" gives the before-and-after demographics for every school on four measures — economically disadvantaged (EcDis), diversity
t.additional: 1 Pause the current timeline — there is no operational deadline before August 2027. 2 Reject these first draft maps and the process on which they were built as the basis for this and any future recommendation. 3 Re-run the process with Demographics as an explicitly weighted principle, and publish a written equity impact analysis before any vote — school by school, covering poverty/Title I concentration, English-learner and IEP concentration, the differentiated-instruction workload this creates for teachers, and resource disparities such as PTA fundraising. 4 Evaluate a capacity-addition alternative that puts elementary capacity where the growth actually is (the north/Stonehouse area), rather than absorbing localized overcrowding through a division-wide demographic reshuffle — including revisiting the tenth elementary school the division once called "urgent." 5 Commit, in writing, not to raise any school's economic-disadvantage or segregation level without a stated public justification you agree and are willing to defend live, in public. 6 Hold a genuine, public Q&A before any future recommendations are drafted or released, much less recommended to the Board. I am not asking the Board to stop planning for population growth and shifts. I am asking it to honor this community’s history, our empathy, the board’s own principle, to use its own data, and not solve a problem in the north of the county by deepening segregation across the entire division. I am concerned about the timing of this proposed redistricting. It would make far more sense to defer implementation until the fall of 2029. Pushing the start date back would provide relief to the “pandemic babies” who were 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-grade students when the pandemic hit in 2020. These were critical years for socialization and for developing foundational reading, writing, and math skills. Missing much of that experience had a tremendous impact, one that is still showing up on a large scale through testing results and other measures. The mental health and developmental needs of these students should be a central consideration, as they suffered immeasurably during their formative years within the WJCC educational system because of COVID. If the redistricting takes place in the fall of 2027, many of these students could have their WJCC experience bookended by two incredibly stressful and mentally taxing disruptions, including the possibility of being required to change high schools in the middle of that critical four-year experience. Prioritizing the mental health of students, as well as recognizing the extraordinary demands placed on teachers and staff, should remain a key consideration. Educators were forced to rapidly adapt their teaching methods while supporting students who fell behind academically and socially due to the pandemic. The strain on everyone involved has been immense. Teachers were pushed to their limits, and the school system lost many outstanding educators who either changed careers or took early retirement. The pandemic was unpredictable and beyond anyone’s control, but the timing of these proposed redistricting changes is entirely within the control of the school board and the consulting firm. It should also be noted that the stress and uncertainty surrounding redistricting are already affecting students, families, and teachers as they consider these possible changes and the possibility of being forced to switch schools during high school. Additionally, with the large-scale “principal swap,” 7 of the 16 WJCC schools will have new principals next year. That alone will create a significant adjustment for many students, teachers, and families. Several of the principals being reassigned are long-standing and deeply respected leaders who helped guide their schools through particularly challenging periods in the past.

t.critical: I already completed this survey once but am repeating it because of Daniel Cheever’s recent comments. I previously believed that the redistricting efforts aimed to maintain racial-ethnic and socioeconomic diversity across schools while addressing building capacity and eliminating geographic inefficiencies. I no longer feel comfortable assuming this is the case. I need to see projected racial-ethnic and socioeconomic diversity for schools before I am able to comment. I think diversity is an independent good that enhances the learning experiences of all students, and that we should not reify differences by assuming students will be comfortable if they are redistricting to attend school predominantly with people who physically resemble them. I think the most uncomfortable scenario is for non White students to be concentrated in specific schools, so that students of different backgrounds do not have the opportunity to learn from each other’s perspective, and so that a small number of non White students are isolated in a community without adequate representation. I also think it is critical to balance socioeconomic disadvantage across schools, so that the resources and services of any one school are not overtaxed by level of need.

t.additional: I oppose redistricting as a solution to school overcrowding because it shifts the burden of growth onto families and children who have already established strong connections to their schools, teachers, and communities. The current enrollment challenges are largely the result of years of rapid residential growth, high-density housing approvals, and inadequate long-term infrastructure planning. Families purchased homes and invested in neighborhoods with the expectation that their children would attend local schools. Redistricting disrupts those expectations, separates students from friends and community networks, and can create unnecessary stress and instability during critical educational years. Rather than repeatedly moving students to address capacity issues, the county should focus on long-term solutions that better align future development with school capacity planning and infrastructure investments.

Dear Members of the WJCC School Board and the Redistricting Steering Committee, As a resident of the Wellington neighborhood and the parent of current and graders at Stonehouse Elementary (and also a grader at Toano Middle), I am writing to express my strong opposition to the draft proposal that would rezone our neighborhood to Norge Elementary beginning in the 2027-2028 school year. While I understand that the opening of the new Bright Beginnings Pre-K centers requires the division to reevaluate building capacity and boundaries, removing Wellington from the Stonehouse attendance zone directly contradicts several of the guiding principles established by WJCC and MGT for this redistricting process. I respectfully ask that you keep the Wellington neighborhood zoned for Stonehouse Elementary for the following reasons: 1. Geographic Proximity and Transportation Efficiency One of the committee's primary goals is to improve transportation efficiency and minimize student travel times. Geographically, Stonehouse is our true neighborhood school. The drive from Wellington to Stonehouse is a short, direct route. Rerouting our children to Norge Elementary forces buses to travel further down the heavily trafficked Route 60 (Richmond Road) corridor. At a time when the division is looking to optimize bus routes and driver resources, it is counterintuitive to bypass a school right in our backyard to bus young children further away. 2. Minimizing Disruption During a Critical Academic Transition The proposed change would take effect during the 2027-2028 school year, which will be my son's third-grade year—as well as the third-grade year for all current first graders in Wellington. Third grade is widely recognized as one of the most critical transition years in elementary education. It marks the shift from "learning to read" to "reading to learn" and introduces the pressure of standardized SOL testing. Uprooting these children from the teachers, administrative staff, and peer support systems they have known since Kindergarten—right as they face increased academic rigor—creates an unnecessary hurdle to their success. 3. Preserving Neighborhood Schools and Community Fabric WJCC has emphasized the importance of preserving neighborhood schools. Wellington has deep, established roots within the Stonehouse community. Our children have grown up together, our families are active in the PTA, and our neighborhood identity is closely tied to our current school. Redrawing the lines to sever Wellington from Stonehouse does not just move numbers on a spreadsheet; it fractures a well-established community fabric and penalizes families who specifically chose this neighborhood for its direct proximity to Stonehouse. I recognize that Stonehouse is currently operating over capacity and that difficult decisions must be made. However, balancing the numbers should not come at the cost of common-sense geography and the well-being of our students. Keeping Wellington at Stonehouse ensures the most efficient use of transportation, preserves our neighborhood's community ties, and protects our current early-elementary students from a highly disruptive mid- grade transition. 4. Emotional Impact on Students/Families: Many of WJCC families and students are associated with the military and or the federal government. These families have had to move, change schools, and restart countless times. The proposed Redistricting would force a number of this population to suffer through another major change, one that is avoidable. As a mother of children who have had to change schools often due to my husband’s career, I am disheartened at this prospect. As a who works closely with military families, I am concerned about the emotional impact and undue stress this change could cause for families who have already sacrificed so much for our country (especially at VA Purple Star schools). Thank you for your time, your service to our community, and for taking the concerns of Wellington families into consideration before making a final recommendation this fall. Sincerely,

t.additional: I am writing to express my concern with the proposed Middle School Maps. I come at this from the perspective of a parent who lives in the Rolling Woods neighborhood, . Our neighborhood is currently zoned for Laurel Lane Elementary School, which is just down the street, and for Berkeley Middle School. Under the proposed map, we would remain zoned for Laurel Lane, which makes sense, as children from our neighborhood would have to drive by Laurel Lane to get to any other elementary school, but for middle school, we are shown as being rezoned for James Blair. I have no objection to James Blair as a school, but I think this is an error that will lead to inefficient bussing. I understand that part of the rationale behind the new map is that it creates a “contiguous” zone for James Blair, which had previously been divided between two non-contiguous zones. While the proposed James Blair and Berkeley Zones appear to be contiguous when you look at them on the map, they are not when you take the roads into account. For example, the HollyBrook and Rolling Woods neighborhoods look like they are right next to each other on the map. In reality, there is no direct way to cross from one to another. To get to Hollybrook from Rolling Woods, one must take Lake Powell Road all the way to where it meets 199 and then take 199 and Jamestown road to get to Hollybrook. This becomes most problematic when one considers that the neighborhoods just South of Rolling Woods have been zoned for Berkeley Middle School. If one simply looks overhead on the map, the Berkeley Zone looks like it constitutes a neat, contiguous zone that runs along the James River, from Jamestown Road through neighborhoods like the Vineyards and then to Kingspoint and Kingsmill. In reality, these neighborhoods are isolated from each other. For instance, to pick up the children in the Vineyards, just a bit south of Rolling Woods, the Berkeley bus will need to come in from route 199 and drive down Lake Powell Road, past a bunch of neighborhoods (including ours) that are zoned for James Blair, and then come back out the same way. There is no other way to get between the Vineyards and James Blair. Lake Powell Road to 199 is the only way in and out (it is worth noting that, for someone not familiar with the area, it may appear that there is a second way in and out, by taking Lake Powell Road to Neck- o-land Road and then to Jamestown Road. That does not actually work, however, as Lake Powell Road is broken in the middle by Lake Powell. The part of Lake Powell Road that connects to Neck-o-land Road and then to Jamestown Road does not connect to the part of Lake Powell Road that we are on). That means that at roughly the same time the children in Rolling Woods are being picked up by the James Blair Middle School bus, a Berkeley Middle School bus will be passing by our neighborhood twice, on the way in and the way out. In short, it does not make sense to split the neighborhoods along Lake Powell Road between two different middle schools. It will duplicate bussing efforts, when we are already so short of drivers. I should also point out that on the other end, to get to James Blair Middle School from our neighborhood, the bus would literally have to drive by Berkeley. My second major concern has to do with utilization and capacity. Slides 52 and 53 helpfully provide projections of the percentage of capacity that will be utilized under the current map and the revised map. I understand that the primary concern here is that Toano is projected to be over capacity by 2035 if the district boundaries remain as they are, and I appreciate the district’s efforts to alleviate that problem. I do not, understand, however, how the proposed boundaries effectively deal with capacity at the other middle schools. According to slide 53, under the proposed map, by 2035, James Blair would be operating at 90% of capacity while Berkeley would be operating at just 68%. That seems remarkably inefficient, and actually does worse than the current map, which would have James Blair at 84% and Berkeley at 74% in 2035. The proposed map, in effect, moves students from less crowded schools to more crowded schools, exacerbating the differences. It seems like the goal should be to move students from Toano, the most crowded school, to Berkeley and Hornsby, the least. I am not sure why students are being moved out of Berkeley based on these numbers. I should also say that I was disappointed when I looked at the statistics presented by the Village Initiative to see that the new map would deepen economic inequalities in the district, given that one of the guiding principles of the redistricting was to “Consider racial and ethnic diversity, as well as socioeconomic indicators, within schools.” I know teachers at Matthew Whaley, and I know from them that Matthew Whaley’s resources are stretched thin, but the current map would have them moving from 45.7% of their population being economically disadvantaged to 54.3%, while Matoaka, already known in the district as an affluent school, would go from 24.8% to 16.8%. English- language learners would be more heavily concentrated at James River and Matthew Whaley elementary schools, which already have heavy concentrations. I began writing this comment before the controversy over the superintendent’s comments at LaFayette High School. I have to say that after those comments and the superintendent’s shifting responses to them (which, as a side note, I thought did a poor job of modelling accountability for our district’s students), my trust in the process that produced these maps is low. I sincerely hope the district will go back to the drawing board and start over.

t.critical: I am deeply concerned that the proposed boundary changes are being presented as improving student “distribution” without sufficient transparency about their actual goals, supporting data, or educational consequences. The plan appears to use students as tools to rebalance demographics and manipulate school performance metrics - concentrating students who, to paraphrase our illustrious superintendent, “look more like each other,” while moving students from higher-performing neighborhoods into lower-performing schools to raise aggregate scores. Regardless of the stated intent, families deserve an honest explanation of how race, socioeconomic status, academic performance, transportation, school capacity, and continuity were weighted in these decisions. School boundaries should be determined by what provides every child with the strongest educational experience - not by efforts to engineer demographic groupings or improve performance statistics on paper. Before making changes that could significantly disrupt students, families, and communities, the district should publish its complete methodology, projected school-level outcomes, and all alternative options considered.

These boundary changes would be unnecessary had the Division adequately anticipated the area’s continued population growth and planned for the addition of one or two elementary schools where capacity is actually needed. This is also a poor reflection of the Division’s ability to work effectively with James City County and the Commonwealth to secure the facilities and resources necessary to serve the communities you represent. Families should not be forced to absorb the consequences of years of inadequate planning. Shame on you. And before the Division or County cites a lack of funding as justification, it should explain why public resources were prioritized for an extraordinarily expensive new county office complex while the need for additional schools went unaddressed. Funding limitations are not a credible excuse when the County has demonstrated that substantial resources can be found for other capital projects. The issue is not simply a lack of money; it is a failure to prioritize schools, students, and the communities experiencing this continued growth.

t.concern: The potential loss of socioeconomic and racial diversity across multiple elementary schools—particularly Matoaka, Stonehouse, Laurel Lane, and Norge—and the increased concentration of poverty and student need in others, including DJ Montague, James River,
t.additional: As the parent of a child zoned for Matoaka, my biggest concern is that the proposed boundary changes appear likely to reduce racial and socioeconomic diversity throughout my child’s educational pathway. Currently, Matoaka already has one of the lowest percentages of students of color and one of the lowest percentages of economically disadvantaged students in the division. Under the proposed maps, those numbers would decline even further, making Matoaka the least racially diverse elementary school in the division and one of the least socioeconomically diverse as well. For that reason, I understand why many families already view Matoaka as the division’s “country club” school, and I am concerned that the proposed boundaries would only reinforce that reality. I want my child to attend schools that reflect the broader community and provide meaningful opportunities to learn alongside peers from different racial, cultural, and socioeconomic backgrounds. Those experiences help students build empathy, understanding, and friendships across differences and better prepare them for life in an increasingly diverse society. My concern does not end at the elementary level. Under the proposed middle school boundaries, my child’s zoned middle school would change from James Blair to Hornsby. Based on the projected demographics, James Blair would become more diverse while Hornsby would become less diverse both racially and socioeconomically. As a result, my child would have fewer opportunities to learn alongside and build relationships with peers from different backgrounds. While the proposed maps do not change my child’s zoned high school, Lafayette, I am concerned about the broader pattern that continues at the high school level. Under the proposed maps, Lafayette would serve an even greater share of the division’s students of color and economically disadvantaged students, while Jamestown would remain the division’s whitest and most affluent high school. This raises concerns about whether the proposal is promoting greater integration and opportunity across schools or further concentrating need in certain schools while concentrating affluence in others. I recognize that enrollment balance and capacity are important considerations. However, I hope the Division also carefully considers the long-term impact of these changes on diversity, equity, and student opportunity. I would like the Division to address several questions: Has the district analyzed potential impacts on Title I status and related supports? How will additional resources be allocated if poverty becomes more concentrated? What is the justification for making already affluent schools wealthier while concentrating need elsewhere? How were diversity and equity weighed against other goals in developing the maps? My recommendation is that the Division explore alternatives that better preserve racial and socioeconomic diversity and avoid increasing concentrations of poverty and affluence within particular schools.

t.critical: Equity across schools. WJCC School district should not create “rich” schools and “poor schools” or “white schools” and “non-white schools.” Feeder patterns that keep neighborhoods together do just this. WJCC neighborhoods are segregated. Public schools should be places where people from all parts of life come together. We should want students to engage with people from outside of their neighborhoods.
t.concern: This creates segregated schools. It essentially places the most economically disadvantaged kids in James River, Matthew Whaley, and DJ Montague while makes the wealthy schools (Matoaka) wealthier. PTA dollars will be highly skewed across schools. In addit
t.additional: Three things… 1) I’m not sure why WJCC School Division would want to so heavily concentrate disadvantaged students in the same schools. Basing redistricting on neighborhood feeder patterns creates segregated schools. Why? Because WJCC neighborhoods are segregated. Public schools should be a place where people from all parts of our community interact with one another, not with just the kids from their neighborhood. We should not willing segregate our schools. Doing so will not only likely deepen achievement gaps, but also prevent students from seeing and understanding the world of difference in which we live. 2) The K-12 student population forecasts seem incorrect. According to MGT’s data, there will be 100-200 fewer students enrolled in the WJCC school district by 2035. All the projections I’ve seen elsewhere show the JCC population increasing by 11,000 people by 2030 and nearly 20,000 people by 2040. In addition, Williamsburg is expected to grow by 700 people by 2030 and 2000 people by 2040. Given a projected 22,000 person population increase by 2040, it doesn’t make sense that the student population would decline (see for example https://www.coopercenter.org/virginia-population-projections). I strongly suggest MGT revisit their model. The discrepancies between their projections and those elsewhere are pretty extreme. 3) MGT’s growth projections largely only account for new neighborhoods/housing that will be built. However, a major source of new students in WJCC is in places of temporary living and/or converted hotels. How does MGT account for these sites of student growth?
